title: Get workshop-ready: your AI agent on your laptop · hancrafted
description: A step-by-step guide for first-timers on Mac, Windows or Linux: open your terminal, install and sign in to your AI agent, start it in the starter folder and run your first skill, so the workshop can begin right away.

The technical route (1/1) Page 1 of 1 Set up the Matt Pocock skills yourself Five lines in an empty folder of your own. Skip the starter zip: it would bring the Matt Pocock skills a second time. Help Your error Copy prompt ChatGPT Gemini 1 Install Node.js The skills installer runs on it. Take the version the page recommends. Node.js · official download page (opens in a new tab) 2 Add the main Matt Pocock skills In your terminal. When it asks which skills, keep the main group and leave Other unticked. $ npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills ? Which skills do you want to install? mattpocock-skills main group, with the setup skill Other misc · in-progress, not needed 3 Run his setup skill in your AI agent It asks a few questions, one at a time. Give these four answers. ✻ > /setup-matt-pocock-skills 1 · Issue tracker Local markdown, no GitHub 2 · Domain docs A single GLOSSARY.md 3 · Triage labels Keep the defaults 4 · Which file AGENTS.md , plus a CLAUDE.md holding @AGENTS.md 4 Add our check and the hancrafted entry The only two pieces from us. Unzip the skill into the skills folder the installer made; paste the entry into GLOSSARY.md , or create the file with it. hancrafted-check-setup · skill folder only small zip GLOSSARY.md · add this entry **hancrafted**: Han's workshop homepage, https://hancrafted.net 5 Run the same check as step 4 It confirms the Matt Pocock skills are in place. Approve its command, and the hancrafted homepage opens. ✻ > /hancrafted-check-setup hancrafted.net hancrafted The homepage opens

Overview Minimal still needs a way out A minimal manual, centred on real tasks, taught faster than a standard manual in a study of 64 students, but beginners still need error-recovery material, which is why every step has a Stuck? help 1 2 . Sources (2) Lazonder and van der Meij, The minimal manual: is less really more? ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Kalyuga, Ayres, Chandler and Sweller, The Expertise Reversal Effect ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org

Open your terminal Hesitation is normal Computer anxiety is a long-studied, widespread reaction; about 80% of the 89 studies on experience found more experience went with less anxiety, and a relaxed first experience was linked to lower anxiety. No study measures fear of the terminal itself, so applying this to the terminal is an inference 1 . Sources (1) Powell, Computer anxiety: Comparison of research from the 1990s and 2000s ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Why the command line feels scary System administrators said you cannot click your way around a command line to figure it out, and that it may be scary or overwhelming for a beginner; this is a survey quote, not a measured rate of mistakes 1 . Sources (1) Voronkov, Martucci and Lindskog, System Administrators Prefer Command Line Interfaces, Don't They? An Exploratory Study of Firewall Interfaces ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Setup is the hard part Software Carpentry reports that installing software is often harder than using it, and that every new tool fails for at least one person in the room across Mac, Windows and Linux 1 . Sources (1) Wilson, Software Carpentry: lessons learned ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Feedback builds confidence In a university Unix course with near-instant per-answer feedback, 78.2% of 2021 respondents said they had procedural Unix knowledge, against 38.8% before; the authors call this self-report possibly subjective, and the students were not solo first-timers 1 . Sources (1) Berry et al., ShellOnYou: learning by doing Unix command line ( opens in a new tab ) ctiber.github.io

What you're looking at Try it and see In a university Unix course with near-instant feedback on every attempt, 78.2% of 2021 respondents said they had procedural Unix knowledge, against 38.8% before; the authors call this self-report possibly subjective, and the students were not solo first-timers 1 . Run your first skill The prompt is a safeguard, not an error A model can be steered by text it reads, such as a web page or a project file, so OWASP recommends requiring a human to approve high-impact actions; each vendor builds that approval into its default mode 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 . Sources (7) OWASP, LLM01: Prompt Injection ( opens in a new tab ) genai.owasp.org OWASP, LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency ( opens in a new tab ) genai.owasp.org OpenAI, Codex: Agent approvals and security ( opens in a new tab ) learn.chatgpt.com Google, Gemini CLI: Policy engine ( opens in a new tab ) geminicli.com GitHub, About GitHub Copilot CLI ( opens in a new tab ) docs.github.com Google, Antigravity: Permissions ( opens in a new tab ) antigravity.google Anthropic, Claude Code: Configure permissions ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com Claude Code's prompt In manual mode, commands outside a built-in read-only set trigger a "Bash command" dialog asking "Do you want to proceed?" with Yes, "Yes, and don't ask again" and No. Prompt names and defaults differ by AI agent and version and change often, so recheck before showing one on screen 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Claude Code: Configure permissions ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com Why approvals are kept Anthropic says broad file access is risky especially under prompt injection; this is a vendor statement, not an independent study 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Making Claude Code more secure and autonomous with sandboxing ( opens in a new tab ) anthropic.com

Your terminal 0:00 – 0:09 Hook You have never opened a terminal. By the end of this page you will have run your first skill in one. 0:09 – 0:37 Why this page I split this into one step per screen, because a long setup guide feels like a wall and a single step feels like something you can finish. Every step hands you one thing that works and the next step needs it, so when you arrive at the workshop, we can start with a grilling session right away and nobody spends the first hour on setup.

Overview 0:00 – 0:27 Four steps, one chain Here is the whole route in four steps: a terminal, an AI agent, a folder and a skill. Each step only works because the one before it works, so when the last one runs, you know the whole chain holds. It takes about twenty minutes. Tick what you already have, and the card on the right tells you which step to start at. 0:27 – 0:47 Skip what you have Tick the boxes you already have, like an installed AI agent, and the card jumps you to the first step that is still open. And if you would rather build the setup yourself than download it, the last Section is for you, so skip to the end.

Open your terminal 0:00 – 0:30 Not a personal failing If opening a terminal feels a little odd, that is a common reaction, and I would not read it as a sign that you are bad with computers. I think the fear comes from the blank window that gives you no hint what to press, and that is my hypothesis, not a proven fact. Nothing here asks you to prove anything, we only open the window and look at it. 0:30 – 0:54 One window, one cursor Pick your system in the toolbar, then open Terminal on a Mac, PowerShell on Windows, or the terminal on Linux. It takes one shortcut and a few letters. You will see a mostly empty window with a blinking cursor, and that is exactly what success looks like here. It is not frozen, it is waiting for you. 0:54 – 1:23 Stuck? Paste it If something looks different on your screen, you do not have to work it out alone. Press Help at the top right of the slide, paste what you see, and it wraps your system, your AI agent and the step into a prompt you can hand to a free ChatGPT or Gemini. Every step has that button, so asking for help is part of the route.

What you're looking at 0:00 – 0:17 Five parts This is what the window you just opened is made of, and there are only five parts: the prompt, the cursor, the command you type, the answer the computer prints, and the close button. That is the whole picture. 0:17 – 0:37 Point at anything Point at any part, or tap it, and a short explanation appears. If you prefer, use Next and Previous and walk through them one by one. The prompt says it is ready, the cursor shows where your typing lands, and the answer comes back right under your command. 0:37 – 0:54 You can't break it Here is the part I would like you to remember: you cannot break anything by looking around in here. If you ever feel lost, close the window, and everything in it ends. Open a new one whenever you like.
Your AI agent 0:00 – 0:14 Terminal done So you now have a window that waits for words. Because an empty window cannot do much on its own, the next piece is the AI agent that will live inside it.

Install your AI agent 0:00 – 0:19 Your first command This is the first command you type in your terminal. It installs your AI agent. Pick your computer and your AI agent in the toolbar, and the page shows you the exact line. Press the big Copy button, paste into your terminal and press Enter. 0:19 – 0:42 Official docs, always Next to the line is a button to the official docs of your AI agent. I give you the line so you do not have to scroll through a page that has no anchor, but the vendor is the source, so if the line ever stops working, the docs are one click away. 0:42 – 1:22 What you will see at the end At the end of the install, your terminal may ask you a question. For Codex on Mac and Linux it is Start Codex now, with y or N: type y and press Enter to go straight to the sign-in. Just pressing Enter means no, and then you open a new terminal and type codex. For GitHub Copilot, answer y if it asks to add itself to your shell file; the last line says copilot help, but you type copilot. For Claude Code you see Installation complete; open a new terminal and type claude. 1:22 – 1:45 What might happen A few things can go wrong, and they are listed under the line for your AI agent. On Windows the usual one is the wrong window: PowerShell and Command Prompt need different lines. If you see red text you do not understand, press Help at the top right, paste the error, and ask.

Log in 0:00 – 0:22 Open a new terminal window Before you type anything, close your terminal and open a new one. The install put your AI agent on your computer, but the old window does not know it yet. If your terminal says command not found or not recognized, this is why. Step one shows you how to open a terminal. 0:22 – 0:44 Your second command Your second command starts your AI agent. Press Copy, paste it and press Enter. Your browser opens for the sign-in; if it does not, the terminal shows a link you can open yourself. Log in with your own account, not a shared one. You do this once, and it stays. 0:44 – 1:19 Which option do I pick? The sign-in asks you to choose, and the page lists the options in the order your AI agent shows them, with one marked Pick this. For Codex it is Sign in with ChatGPT, if you pay for ChatGPT. For Claude Code it is your Claude account. For GitHub Copilot you choose GitHub.com and then the device code. For Antigravity you use your personal Google Account. Afterwards you may be asked whether you trust the folder: say yes only for the starter folder.

Your folder 0:00 – 0:17 Terminal and AI agent, now the place to work You have a terminal and an AI agent, so what is missing is a place to work. An AI agent works inside one folder and reads what is there, so we give it one on purpose: the starter folder.

Download and unzip the starter folder 0:00 – 0:24 One link, one zip There is one link to one zip file. Download it, and then unzip it. On a Mac, double-click the zip. On Windows, right-click it and choose Extract All. On Linux, use Extract here in your file manager. Inside you will find the files the workshop needs, already in place, so there is nothing to assemble. 0:24 – 0:37 Where it lives Take a second to notice where the folder landed, usually in your Downloads. The next step goes into exactly this folder, so if you remember where it is, the rest is easy.

Start the agent inside that folder 0:00 – 0:26 Go in, then start In your terminal you first move into the unzipped folder, and only then you start your AI agent. The page draws the terminal at each point, so you can check that the folder name appears in front of your cursor before you start. The AI agent may ask whether you trust this folder. For this one, you do, so say yes. 0:26 – 0:50 Same folder every time The order matters because an AI agent reads what is in the folder it starts in. That is how it will find your skill in a moment, and if you start it somewhere else, the skill is simply not there. So whenever you work with this starter folder, start the AI agent from inside it. 0:50 – 1:05 Chain so far Look at what you have. A terminal that waits, an AI agent inside it, and a folder it can read. One piece is left, and it is the one that proves all the others work.

Your first skill 0:00 – 0:17 Everything in place So everything is in place: a terminal, an AI agent and a folder. What is left is a skill, which is a small set of instructions your AI agent can follow, and running it shows that the chain is real.

Run your first skill 0:00 – 0:18 Type the skill Type the name of the skill, hancrafted-check-setup, and your AI agent reads it. Before it does anything on your computer, it stops and asks you. That pause is not an error, it is the AI agent handing the decision to you. 0:18 – 0:44 Say yes You are the one who decides here, so look at what it wants to run. For this skill, it opens one web page, and the answer is yes. If you were ever unsure what a command does, you could ask the AI agent to explain it before you approve. Would you rather have a tool that asks, or one that does not? 0:44 – 1:09 The proof Approve it, and the hancrafted homepage opens in your browser. That is the whole check, and there is nothing more to submit. You just ran a skill, so see you at the workshop, and until then, have a look around hancrafted. If the page does not open, the skill prints the link, and you can open it by hand.

The technical route 0:00 – 0:18 For people who build This last Section is for people who build, and it is optional. If you are comfortable with a terminal, you can get the same result without the starter folder by installing the pieces yourself. Everyone else can stop at the homepage.

Set up the Matt Pocock skills yourself 0:00 – 0:27 Same chain, built by hand What the starter folder did for you comes down to four short steps. You install Node.js from its official page, add the Matt Pocock skills, run his setup skill so everything stays local without a GitHub account, and then run the check. The exact lines are on the page, because I would rather you copy them from there than hear them from me. 0:27 – 0:45 Same proof The proof is the same as before. You run hancrafted-check-setup, and the hancrafted homepage opens. One thing to know: that skill comes with the starter folder, not with the Matt Pocock skills, so the page tells you where to take it from.
